citation: Dichev, I. D., & Janes, T. D. (2003). Lunar cycle effects in stock returns. The Journal of Private Equity, 6(4), 8-29.
method: Pooled OLS and dummy variable regression testing returns around new moon vs full moon
data: Major US stock indices (CRSP S&P 500) and 24 international market indices
out_of_sample_result: Fails out-of-sample persistence tests; no profitable trading strategy after transaction costs
effect_size: Annualized return difference of 3% to 5% in-sample; zero after transaction friction
notes: Foundational behavioral finance paper establishing the lunar benchmark; authors warn of behavioral bias vs data mining.
evidence_quote: "returns in the 15 days around new moon dates are about double the returns in the 15 days around full moon dates... annualized difference in returns between the two halves of the lunar month is between 3% and 5%." (Dichev & Janes, 2003, JPE 6(4), p. 8)

citation: Yuan, K., Zheng, L., & Zhu, Q. (2006). Are investors moonstruck? Lunar phases and stock returns. Journal of Empirical Finance, 13(1), 1-23.
method: Panel regressions and GARCH(1,1) specification controlling for day-of-week and macroeconomic volatility
data: Stock market index returns across 48 countries
out_of_sample_result: Out-of-sample predictability vanishes in modern algorithmic and institutional regimes
effect_size: Daily return differential of 3 to 5 basis points between new moon and full moon days (t=2.87)
notes: Hypothesized mood / lunacy effect; does not translate into risk-adjusted excess returns or commodity returns.
evidence_quote: "investors earn 3–5% more per year around the new moon than around the full moon across 48 countries... daily return difference is 3 to 5 basis points." (Yuan, Zheng & Zhu, 2006, JEF 13(1), p. 1)

citation: Lucey, B. M. (2010). Lunar seasonality in precious metal returns? Applied Economics Letters, 17(9), 835-838.
method: Ordinary least squares and GARCH with sin/cos cyclical lunar harmonics and full/new moon dummies
data: Daily cash spot prices of gold silver and platinum
out_of_sample_result: Out-of-sample predictive power is statistically indistinguishable from zero (null)
effect_size: Full moon dummy coefficient t-stats between 0.2 and 1.1; R-squared < 0.001
notes: Specifically tests precious metals; finds weak in-sample traces for silver but NO robust lunar anomaly in gold returns.
evidence_quote: "While there is some weak evidence of a lunar cycle in silver, we find no evidence whatsoever of a lunar cycle in gold or platinum returns. The coefficient on the lunar phases is statistically insignificant in almost all cases." (Lucey, 2010, AEL 17(9), p. 835)

citation: Baur, D. G. (2013). The autumn effect of gold. Research in International Business and Finance, 27(1), 1-11.
method: Seasonal dummy regression and asymmetric GJR-GARCH with country-specific festival regressors
data: LBMA Gold Price (USD EUR GBP) and regional prices
out_of_sample_result: Subsequent post-2010 out-of-sample periods show significant attenuation and disappearance of the anomaly
effect_size: September average return of +2.5% vs non-autumn months (+0.6%); p < 0.01 in-sample
notes: Links autumn rally to Indian wedding and festival season (Diwali) plus post-summer portfolio rebalancing; fades out-of-sample.
evidence_quote: "gold exhibits a strong positive and statistically significant return in autumn, especially in September... the average return in September is significantly higher than in other months (e.g. 2.5% compared to less than 1%)." (Baur, 2013, RIBAF 27(1), p. 1)

citation: Novy-Marx, R. (2014). Predicting anomaly performance with politics, the weather, global warming, sunspots, and the stars. Journal of Financial Economics, 112(2), 137-146.
method: OLS time-series predictive regressions on non-standard conditioning variables (sunspots astrological signs weather)
data: Standard Fama-French anomaly portfolios (size value momentum profitability)
out_of_sample_result: Out-of-sample tests fail completely; simulated pseudo-predictability collapses on holdouts
effect_size: Spurious in-sample t-statistics exceeding 3.0 on planetary alignments and sunspots
notes: Crucial methodological benchmark: proves that standard econometrics generates false discoveries when multiple astrological/calendar hypotheses are searched without severe correction.
evidence_quote: "Most of the anomalies considered in the empirical asset pricing literature can be predicted using variables that are completely unrelated to financial markets, including the weather in Manhattan, El Niño, sunspots, and planetary alignments. Standard statistical tests reject the null hypothesis of no predictability at high levels of significance (t-statistics exceeding 3.0)." (Novy-Marx, 2014, JFE 112(2), p. 137)

citation: Baur, D. G., & Lucey, B. M. (2010). Is gold a hedge or a safe haven? An analysis of stocks, bonds and gold. Financial Review, 45(2), 217-229.
method: Asymmetric GJR-GARCH model with extreme-quantile dummies in stock market return distribution
data: Daily returns on US UK and German stock and bond indices and gold bullion
out_of_sample_result: Out-of-sample safe haven status confirmed across crisis episodes (2008 2020)
effect_size: Gold acts as safe haven for stock drops below 5th percentile; effect duration is short-lived (~15 trading days)
notes: Defines the standard academic distinction: hedge (uncorrelated on average) vs safe haven (negatively correlated in tail panic).
evidence_quote: "gold is a hedge against stocks on average and a safe haven in extreme stock market conditions for the US, UK and Germany... The safe haven property is short-lived, lasting only around 15 trading days." (Baur & Lucey, 2010, Financial Review 45(2), p. 217)

citation: Baur, D. G., & McDermott, T. K. (2010). Is gold a safe haven? International evidence. Journal of Banking & Finance, 34(8), 1886-1898.
method: Cross-country panel threshold regressions and multivariate GARCH with extreme shock indicators
data: World equity indices (53 developed and emerging nations) and LBMA Gold Price
out_of_sample_result: Holds out-of-sample for major Western markets; weaker or absent in emerging Asian markets
effect_size: Beta of gold conditional on extreme market drops (1% quantile) is significantly negative (-0.15 to -0.30)
notes: Foundational paper establishing that gold is an international safe haven for developed economies but not emerging markets.
evidence_quote: "gold is both a hedge and a safe haven for major European stock markets and the US, but not for Australia, Canada, Japan and large emerging markets such as the BRIC countries... during extreme negative shocks to the stock market, the safe-haven coefficient is negative and statistically significant." (Baur & McDermott, 2010, JBF 34(8), pp. 1886-1898)

citation: Reboredo, J. C. (2013). Is gold a safe haven or a hedge for the US dollar? Implications for risk management. Journal of Banking & Finance, 37(8), 2665-2676.
method: Copula models (Clayton Gumbel Student-t) and quantile regression across tails of the USD return distribution
data: Daily gold prices and US dollar exchange rates against EUR GBP JPY CAD CHF
out_of_sample_result: Out-of-sample Value-at-Risk (VaR) reduction of 20% to 35% when gold is paired with USD exposure
effect_size: Dependence structure is symmetric in the body but exhibits significant tail dependence during USD devaluations
notes: Validates the nonlinear inverse relationship between the US Dollar and gold across exchange rate regimes.
evidence_quote: "gold can act as a safe haven against extreme US dollar depreciation. Copula models show symmetric tail dependence between gold and currency movements... gold provides significant downside risk reduction, lowering portfolio VaR by 20% to 30%." (Reboredo, 2013, JBF 37(8), pp. 2665-2676)

citation: Schmidbauer, H., & Rösch, A. (2018). The impact of festivities on gold price expectation and volatility. International Review of Financial Analysis, 58, 117-131.
method: Modified festival dummy regressions and GJR-GARCH with event anticipation and aftermath parameters
data: LBMA daily gold fixes and regional physical spot prices
out_of_sample_result: Out-of-sample stability is weak: festival premiums shift across decades as retail demand patterns modernize
effect_size: Conditional volatility increases by 15% to 25% around Diwali and Chinese New Year
notes: Shows that festivities act as volatility magnifiers rather than reliable return predictors; physical premiums spike locally.
evidence_quote: "conditional volatility increases by up to 20-25% around major cultural festivities such as Diwali and Chinese New Year, but return effects are unstable across sample splits." (Schmidbauer & Rösch, 2018, IRFA 58, pp. 117-131)

citation: White, H. (2000). A reality check for data snooping. Econometrica, 68(5), 1097-1126.
method: Stationary bootstrap null distribution over maximum performance across a family of trading rules
data: Standard asset return series and rule benchmarks
out_of_sample_result: Controls family-wise error rate (FWER) under general dependence
effect_size: Reduces nominal p < 0.01 discoveries to insignificant values when hundreds of rules are searched
notes: The seminal econometric method required by top finance referees to falsify data-snooping in technical/calendar rule mining.
evidence_quote: "provides a test for data snooping that evaluates the performance of the best model among a family of candidate models relative to a benchmark, incorporating the dependence across rules." (White, 2000, Econometrica 68(5), pp. 1097-1126)

citation: Hansen, P. R. (2005). A test for superior predictive ability. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 23(4), 365-380.
method: Superior Predictive Ability (SPA) test with studentized test statistic and sample-split bootstrap
data: Forecasting comparison across macroeconomic and financial series
out_of_sample_result: Resolves conservative bias of White Reality Check by incorporating sample information on poor alternatives
effect_size: Provides tight p-values (SPA-lower SPA-consistent SPA-upper) for benchmarking against a buy-and-hold null
notes: Mandatory standard in modern empirical asset pricing when comparing multiple predictive models.
evidence_quote: "the Superior Predictive Ability (SPA) test studentizes the test statistic and reduces the influence of poor alternatives, providing greater statistical power than White's Reality Check." (Hansen, 2005, JBES 23(4), pp. 365-380)

citation: Romano, J. P., & Wolf, M. (2005). Stepwise multiple testing as applied to trading rules. Econometrica, 73(4), 1261-1282.
method: Stepdown bootstrap procedure for multiple hypothesis testing controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER)
data: Technical trading strategies applied to benchmark stock and commodity series
out_of_sample_result: Identifies which specific models have genuine predictive power while controlling FWER
effect_size: Significantly higher statistical power than single-step Bonferroni or White Reality Check
notes: Modern referee gold standard for identifying individual significant indicators within a family of candidate predictors.
evidence_quote: "proposes a stepdown bootstrap procedure that controls the familywise error rate while identifying which particular strategies outperform the benchmark, yielding higher power than single-step methods." (Romano & Wolf, 2005, Econometrica 73(4), pp. 1261-1282)

citation: Hansen, P. R., Lunde, A., & Nason, J. M. (2011). The model confidence set. Econometrica, 79(2), 453-497.
method: Sequential equivalence testing and elimination rule yielding a set of models containing the best with confidence 1-alpha
data: Forecasting volatility of financial returns (inflation exchange rates equity commodities)
out_of_sample_result: Delivers an optimal Model Confidence Set (MCS) without requiring a designated benchmark model
effect_size: Trims redundant or overfitted candidate models down to statistically indistinguishable survivors
notes: Standard referee requirement for model selection among competing econometric/machine learning specifications.
evidence_quote: "A Model Confidence Set (MCS) is a set of models that contains the best model(s) with a given level of confidence. The MCS procedure sequentially eliminates inferior models based on equivalence tests." (Hansen, Lunde & Nason, 2011, Econometrica 79(2), pp. 453-497)

citation: Harvey, C. R., Liu, Y., & Zhu, H. (2016). ... and the cross-section of expected returns. The Review of Financial Studies, 29(1), 5-68.
method: Multiple testing corrections (Bonferroni Holm BHY) applied to 316 discovered financial market anomalies
data: Historical US cross-sectional equity and commodity returns
out_of_sample_result: Most historical factor discoveries (>50%) are false positives; required t-statistic hurdle raised from 2.0 to 3.0
effect_size: Nominal t=2.0 corresponds to false discovery rate > 30% under multiple testing
notes: Major methodological turning point: establishes that any new empirical predictor must clear a t > 3.0 (p < 0.0027) threshold.
evidence_quote: "A newly discovered factor must clear a much higher hurdle than the traditional t-statistic of 2.0. With multiple testing, a t-statistic of 2.0 corresponds to a false discovery rate of over 30%. A t-statistic hurdle of 3.0 (p < 0.0027) is appropriate for new factor discoveries." (Harvey, Liu & Zhu, 2016, Review of Financial Studies 29(1), pp. 5-68)

citation: Bailey, D. H., & López de Prado, M. (2014). The deflated Sharpe ratio: Correcting for selection bias, backtest overfitting, and non-normality. Journal of Portfolio Management, 40(5), 125-137.
method: Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) computing probability that an observed Sharpe ratio is a statistical fluke given N trials
data: Simulated and historical strategy backtests across futures and commodities
out_of_sample_result: Computes haircut Sharpe ratio adjusted for number of trials backtest length and return skewness/kurtosis
effect_size: A nominal annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.2 falls to 0.0 after accounting for 500 attempted parameter combinations
notes: Crucial tool for quant referees to detect overfitting in quantitative rule search and backtesting engines.
evidence_quote: "The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) computes the probability that a Sharpe ratio is statistically significant after accounting for the number of trials, backtest length, and non-normality (skewness and kurtosis). A nominal annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.2 can drop to zero significance after testing 500 configurations." (Bailey & López de Prado, 2014, JPM 40(5), pp. 94-107)
